script: [serious] Fifty-three minutes before the attack on Pearl Harbor, American radar saw the Japanese planes coming. Nobody sounded the alarm. December 7th, 1941. Seven-oh-two in the morning. On a hilltop in Hawaii called Opana, two young Army privates, Joseph Lockard and George Elliott, were running a new radar set. On the screen appeared the biggest blip Lockard had ever seen. So big he thought the machine was broken. Planes. A lot of them. About a hundred and thirty miles north, and coming closer. Elliott called it in. Large number of planes coming in from the north. The officer on duty, Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, knew a flight of American B-17 bombers was due from California that morning. He told them, don't worry about it. It wasn't the only warning. An hour earlier, the destroyer USS Ward had fired on a Japanese submarine at the harbor entrance, and reported it. At seven fifty-five, the first bombs fell. More than twenty-four hundred Americans were killed. Investigators later cleared Tyler. The radar couldn't tell friend from foe, and nobody had told him a war warning had been issued. Send this to someone who thinks one phone call can't change history. This is Dossier Decoded. Case file number forty-four. A new file every day.
